summary: An informational memo specifying how to encapsulate airline-specific protocols for reservation, ticketing and messaging traffic over IP, so legacy airline systems can run across an IP network.

eli5.summary: Airlines used their own special computer languages. This memo shows how to carry them across the regular internet.

questions: how airline protocols run over ip
how do airlines run legacy protocols over ip
what are type a and type b airline traffic
how does airline traffic map to tcp/ip
subtitle: A TCP/IP encapsulation for legacy airline reservation, ticketing, and messaging protocols.

tldr.problem: Airlines have operated proprietary data networks with specialized protocols (like ALC and UTS) for over 40 years, but many organizations cannot immediately migrate their legacy equipment to modern standards.
tldr.mechanism: MATIP specifies how to encapsulate Type A (transactional) and Type B (messaging) airline traffic into TCP/IP packets, allowing legacy airline systems to operate over standard IP networks without immediate equipment replacement.
tldr.outcome: Airlines gained a way to migrate gradually from proprietary networks to TCP/IP infrastructure, though no major deployments are mentioned in the RFC.

today: RFC 2351 is an Informational document describing a migration pathway for legacy airline systems. The document includes a security disclaimer noting that it fails to adequately address security concerns. MATIP enabled some airlines to bridge their proprietary systems to TCP/IP networks, but widespread adoption was limited. Modern airline systems have largely migrated to contemporary protocols and architectures.

sections.title: Airline Networks and Migration
sections.content:
The airline industry has used a worldwide data network for over 40 years, built on synchronous protocols developed before OSI and SNA standards. Two main traffic types exist: TYPE A (transactional, query-response between terminals and central systems), used for seat reservations and ticket issuing, and TYPE B (messaging with high reliability), used for email-like communications.

Thousands of airline offices worldwide still operate dumb terminals using proprietary protocols like P1024B (IBM ALC) and P1024C (UNISYS UTS). While many airlines want to migrate to standardized protocols to reduce costs, they cannot immediately replace their equipment. This RFC defines a mapping to carry airline traffic over TCP/IP so legacy systems can operate on modern networks while migration proceeds gradually.
sections.eli5: Airlines have old computer systems that speak special languages. Instead of throwing them all away, this system wraps the old languages inside regular internet messages, so old systems can use modern networks.

sections.title: Traffic Types and Session Establishment
sections.content:
MATIP defines session-oriented communication over TCP. A MATIP session is established above the TCP connection to identify traffic characteristics such as the subtype (Type A host-to-host versus Type A conversational), multiplexing mode, data header format, and character set. Each combination of parameters requires a separate session and TCP connection.

Three commands manage the MATIP session: Session Open (SO) to initiate a session with configuration parameters, Open Confirm (OC) to accept or reject the SO command, and Session Close (SC) to terminate the session. The TCP connection can remain open even after closing the MATIP session, allowing new sessions to be established on the same connection.

For TYPE A conversational traffic, sessions identify terminals (called ASCUs) and support multiplexing. For TYPE A host-to-host traffic, sessions identify remote hosts independently of IP addresses using H1 H2 identifiers. For TYPE B traffic, identification uses High Level Designators (HLDs) of the sender and recipient systems.
sections.eli5: Before sending any data, the two systems do a handshake to agree on what type of traffic they will send, what language to use, and other settings. Once they agree, they can send data packets, and when done, they close the session.

sections.title: Packet Formats
sections.content:
All MATIP packets begin with a 4-byte header containing a 5-bit reserved field (set to zero), a 3-bit Version field (must be 001), a Control bit (1 for control packets, 0 for data), an 8-bit Command field (only used in control packets), and a 16-bit Length field indicating the total packet size.

Control packets (SO, OC, SC) contain session configuration information. For TYPE A conversational, the SO packet includes the coding (character set: 5-bit padded Baudot, 6-bit IPARS, 7-bit ASCII, or 8-bit EBCDIC), a traffic subtype field, multiplexing mode, header format, presentation format (P1024B, P1024C, or 3270), and optionally a list of configured ASCUs.

Data packets carry an optional ID field (format depends on session parameters) followed by the payload. For TYPE A conversational data, the ID contains the terminal identifier(s); for TYPE A host-to-host, the ID contains the flow identifier; for TYPE B, no ID field is present. All data packet formatting beyond the MATIP header follows IATA standards or bilateral agreements between sender and receiver.
sections.eli5: Messages have a 4-byte prefix saying what type they are and how long they are. Session setup messages include settings like what character set to use. Data messages include a small ID field so the system knows where to deliver the payload.

sections.title: Traffic Identification
sections.content:
For TYPE A conversational traffic, ASCUs (Agent Set Control Units) are identified by either 4 bytes (H1 H2 A1 A2) or 2 bytes (A1 A2), with H1 H2 reserved for session identification when 2-byte mode is used. These identifiers are assigned by the host and remain constant regardless of IP address, allowing dynamic recognition of terminals independent of their network location.

For TYPE A host-to-host traffic, the identification consists of 3 bytes (H1 H2 Flow ID), where H1 H2 identify the remote host bilaterally and Flow ID (range 3F-4F hex) distinguishes different flows within a host-to-host session.

For TYPE B traffic, identification uses HLDs (High Level Designators) which may be carried in the SO command or may be derived directly from IP addresses. MATIP uses TCP port 350 for TYPE A traffic and TCP port 351 for TYPE B traffic, allowing the traffic type to be determined by the port number.
sections.eli5: The system has different ways to identify senders and receivers depending on the type of traffic. Sometimes it uses special codes, sometimes it uses port numbers. This lets the system figure out where messages should go.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The RFC explicitly states that the MATIP protocol itself does not include security mechanisms. Security can be addressed at several levels: at the application level through ASCU configuration or User ID/password verification, at the network level through firewall rules on IP addresses and TCP ports, and optionally through IPSec.

The document notes that traffic can be authenticated using static identifiers or cleartext passwords, neither of which provide strong security. For higher security, compliant implementations may implement IPSec ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) for both control and data packets, with optional replay protection and cipher suites. Implementations may also support IPSec AH (Authentication Header).

The RFC includes a security disclaimer stating that the protocol fails to adequately address security concerns, making security optional rather than mandatory. Cleartext passwords are strongly discouraged but supported for compatibility with clients that lack encryption engines.
sections.eli5: The protocol does not protect messages by itself. Users or networks have to add their own protection using passwords, firewalls, or encryption. Clear-text passwords work but are not recommended because they are not secure.
